Grenades, grief and a deepening political divide: five takeaways from Sonia Gandhi’s newly introduced memoir

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From the assassinations of her husband and mother-in-law to press stonewalling under Modi, Belonging offers an insider’s account of India’s political evolution.
  • In a recent development, few love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi.
  • The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the assassinations of her husband and mother-in-law to press stonewalling under Modi, Belonging offers an insider’s account of India’s political evolution.

In a recent development, few love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.

The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.).

Sources indicate that belonging, published today, contains moving glimpses of Gandhi’s private grief. She writes about the loss of her first child, who died shortly after birth, and the chilling discovery of grenades in a room of their house after Operation Blue Star, the 1984 military operation against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple in Amritsar. She also provides a ringside view of several turbulent chapters in Indian politics, not least the violent assassinations of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, in 1984 and her husband, Rajiv, in 1991.

Her book also revisits some of the darker episodes that have dogged the Gandhi family and the Congress party, including Indira’s imposition of the Emergency in June 1975, a 21-month period during which civil liberties were suspended, political opponents were jailed and the press was gagged, which caused fear and dismay across the country. In Gandhi’s account, it also caused a rift within the family.

Ultimately, Gandhi’s memoir is a vivid record of six decades of India’s political transformation from the Congress-dominated secular republic she moved to in 1968 until today, when Hindu nationalism has become the dominant political force under Narendra Modi.

Here are five key takeaways from her memoir and what they reveal about the state of Indian politics today.

Gandhi has had no real contact with Modi for the last 12 years.

In a recent development, gandhi’s account offers a glimpse of how deep the political polarisation runs in Indian politics today. In one revealing passage, Gandhi writes that she has had “practically no real contact” with Modi in the 12 years he has led the nation. In fact, at times when the two have been in the same rooms, such as the speaker’s small chamber, Modi “tends to look away, avoiding eye contact”, she says. On occasion, she adds, he has asked briefly about her health after a hospital stay.

For her, this breakdown is a departure from the past, when leaders on opposing sides of the aisle “would treat one another with cordiality”. After the 2001 terror attack on parliament, Gandhi immediately called then-BJP prime minister AB Vajpayee to enquire about his safety, a gesture he appreciated.

Gandhi sees an increasingly authoritarian style of politics, in which those in power seek to “belittle and torment” opponents. For years, Gandhi’s son, Rahul, has been the subject of BJP’s ridicule, which calls him Pappu, a derisive term intended to portray him as inexperienced and naive. She adds that similar things are happening elsewhere in the world, an observation that can be read in the context of US President Donald Trump’s use of personal insults and ridicule against opponents.

It’s lonely at the top for India’s female politicians.

India has an illustrious history of women occupying top leadership positions, long before many other democracies. But their rise has often come at a cost – that of loneliness in navigating a male-dominated political world.

In the book, Gandhi describes a 2012 conversation with Hillary Clinton on the countrys’ female leaders and their backgrounds. In her recollections of Indira, she shares that, despite wielding authority, Indira could feel besieged and profoundly alone, and this was particularly acute, Gandhi writes, in the months leading up to the declaration of the Emergency by her mother-in-law.

Gandhi also writes of her own isolation, including when she decided to take on the leadership of the Congress out of a sense of duty to her family’s political legacy.

Those in power are increasingly stonewalling the press.

Among the many ways in which Gandhi charts the erosion of India’s democratic conventions in Belonging, one particularly telling shift is the changed relationship between the media and those in power. She recalls a time when journalists had opportunities to question prime ministers directly.

Recent findings suggest that in 12 years in power, Modi has not addressed a single press conference on his own. He has sat in on one press briefing at the conclusion of an election campaign, and appeared alongside US presidents at joint press encounters after bilateral meetings, where they took questions from the press. Modi has consistently avoided facing journalists in an open forum, and his media interactions have largely been one-on-one interviews with sympathetic, pro-government news anchors or in one much publicised exchange with a Bollywood actor who asked him how he liked to eat mangoes.

The book’s publication has brought renewed attention to concerns about the space for free expression in contemporary India, and the extent to which apprehensions about repercussions may influence what can be noted, written and published.

It has been revealed that penguin Random House India was to publish Gandhi’s memoir but withdrew from the project in August. Gandhi told the Guardian that it was “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and mentioned it had dropped the book after she declined certain suggested edits. Penguin has disputed her account, saying that the suggestion it decided not to publish the book because of refused editorial changes “does not accurately reflect the circumstances”.

The book, released in the US by Alfred A Knopf, is being published in India by HarperCollins.

In June, Penguin had also pulled out of aims to distribute graphic journalist Joe Sacco’s The Once and Future Riot, about the 2013 Muzaffarnagar communal violence. The publisher cited an inaccurate map of India and unresolved citation issues. Sacco, however, blamed the decision on the “current political climate in India”.

She’s had quiet fallouts with the ‘thoroughly dishonest’.

In a recent development, western political memoirs, particularly by former heads of government or senior politicians, are often forthcoming in naming political adversaries, recounting private exchanges and offering candid assessments of colleagues. David Cameron’s 2019 memoir, For the Record, took aim at his former friend, Michael Gove, describing him as “mendacious” and a “foam-flecked Faragist”.

Sources indicate that gandhi, in contrast, is restrained. She writes warmly of the closeness between the Gandhi family and that of Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan, whose parents she lived with when she first moved to India, but she makes no mention of the subsequent estrangement between the two families. In another instance, she does not name the political leader she describes as “thoroughly dishonest” and who she claims she trusted in 1999, when Congress unsuccessfully attempted to form a coalition government.

It has been revealed that art | Art Mumbai runs from 12-15 November at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse. Among the highlights of this year’s edition is artist Baaraan Ijlal’s collaboration with the celebrated lyricist Javed Akhtar, turning his evocative Urdu couplets into paintings. The two will be in conversation with curator Ranjit Hoskote on Friday.

Government | The official bungalow of Andhra Pradesh’s chief minister, N Chandrababu Naidu, was renovated by a government-owned enterprise for Rs 6.5 crore (£518,000), according to the Indian Express (£). The renovation work on the Delhi property included was noted to have had a major makeover.

Film | Bollywood’s ambitious rendering of Hindu epic Ramayana, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Sai Pallavi, was released on 5 November. Touted as the most expensive Indian film ever made, it earned praise from the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw, who described it as “thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular”.

Readers from India and around the world on the festival of lights and tell us how they celebrated.

double quotation markIn India, Diwali comes to you. You can see it in the streets, hear it in the neighbourhood and feel it in the atmosphere. In the UK, it is different. Life carries on around you. But traditions do not have to disappear when you move countries – they can change shape. A small light in a quiet room can carry the same meaning as an entire street illuminated for Diwali. Aman, Plymouth, UK.

Industry observers note that double quotation markMy favorite part of Diwali back home was getting up before sunrise on Narak Chaturdashi and having a ceremonial bath, followed by a breakfast of traditional Marathi Diwali snacks. I have been living abroad for over 10 years now and it’s always a bittersweet time of the year where I miss my family and the general vibe of Diwali in India. But I am trying to build new traditions as one half of an Indian-Austrian couple, which includes trading the traditional boxes of mithai for Manner Schnitten and marzipan. Charu, Germany.

Recent findings suggest that double quotation markThere used to be more of a community spirit to Diwali. As kids, we would be tasked with going door to door, exchanging sweets and snacks with neighbours (sometimes to our great displeasure, because it made for awkward conversation with those we had annoyed with our antics). Nowadays, the celebrations are mostly private. Group celebrations are walled off within exclusive clubs, families light their own fireworks almost competitively, and people send each other sweets through a delivery service. Samyuktha, Chennai.

The government has approved the sale of a 60.7% stake in IDBI bank to Canadian Fairfax Holdings for Rs 52,878 crore (£4.22bn).

It’s hard to take one’s eyes off Muhammed Riswan when he’s at work. The 23-year-old football freestyler from Areekode in Kerala’s Malappuram district conjures tricks with the ball in a delicately choreographed dance. It glides between his feet, next it is rolling on to his back right before he leaps into the air to catch it with one hand.

Recent findings suggest that riswan, who’s been freestyling for eight years, is one of the two Indians to win Instagram Rings 2026 award recognising creators. The other is Chanel model Bhavitha Mandava.

Riswan’s major break came with a video filmed at Keralamkundu waterfall, where he pulled off a freestyle move before gracefully arching the ball into the water. The clip has since clocked more than 600m views. Last year, he was invited to watch his sporting idol, Lionel Messi, play in Argentina.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • "We have resolved a technology matter that delayed flight departures," the airline said in a statement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

United Airlines on Monday remarked it had resolved a "widespread system outage" that briefly affected departing flights.

"We have resolved a technology matter that delayed flight departures," the airline said in a statement. "While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.

A United spokesperson stated there was no indication that the outage was a cyberattack.

The Air Line Pilots Association, which represents pilots for United and other carriers, said in an earlier message to members seen by CNBC that the operational outage was "affecting multiple pilot facing applications" and that United could not "provide outbound flights with final weights.".

United's outage came three days after a nationwide ground stop halted departures across the country for more than four hours, snarling travel and leading to widespread delays and cancellations over the weekend.

Recent findings suggest that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the issues that led to Friday's ground stop on a router in Arkansas that overwhelmed systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control. Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford stated the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over from copper wires to fiber optic.

There were significantly fewer flight delays and cancellations Monday than had been reported Sunday, according to FlightAware data.

There was no indication that United's outage Monday was related to the complications that caused Friday's ground stop.

— CNBC's Leslie Josephs and Phil LeBeau contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If the leaders of this year’s United Nations climate conference achieve one of their big goals, countries will rally behind a fresh global target on expanding the reach of electric power.

The implication: The rest of the world will have to look a lot more like China.

Over the past two decades, China has raced ahead of other industrialized countries, building ultrahigh-voltage power lines, constructing the world’s largest high-speed rail system and filling its roads with electric vehicles. It is sometimes called the first electrostate.

At the same time, countries across the West and in Africa are scarcely more electrified than they were a generation ago.

Sources indicate that that disparity is one of the things the climate conference, known this year as COP31, is campaigning to change. The event’s leaders say the shift is well-suited for a year when the United States’ war in Iran has pinched the global oil and gas supply.

Industry observers note that “Electrification is the answer,” said Murat Kurum, the Turkish environment minister, who is leading the 12-day conference in Antalya, Turkey. “Everyone now understands that energy that you must import is energy that you do not control.”.

Electrification involves replacing technologies that directly burn fossil fuels. That means swapping gas-powered vehicles for E.V.s, for instance, and trading oil-fired furnaces for heat pumps. It also entails looking for electric alternatives to generate the steam and intense heat needed by factories.

#12570. Are Smart Car Seats Worth It? I Tested Two to Find Out (2026)

Are Smart Car Seats Worth It? I Tested Two to Find Out (2026)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that car seats had some pretty humble beginnings.
  • Many car seat manufacturers are adding technology to, for lack of a better term, give parents a second set of eyes.
  • It has been revealed that it sounds appealing, right?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that car seats had some pretty humble beginnings. Even I, an early-’90s baby, slightly recoil every time I see a picture of myself strapped into a flimsy plastic bucket with a loud geometric-print cover that once held my life in its clutches. Car seat design and safety standards have come a long way, and today’s models are quite souped up, with cup holders, rotating bases, and enough bells and whistles to rival an Escalade. And now, they’re getting smart.

Many car seat manufacturers are adding technology to, for lack of a better term, give parents a second set of eyes. Think Bluetooth-connected chest clips, sensors, apps, and real-time alerts that ping your phone if something goes awry, whether that’s an installation matter or if a chest clip comes unbuckled while the car’s moving.

It has been revealed that it sounds appealing, right? Especially for parents who already have plenty to worry about and are often juggling a million things just to get out the door in the morning. But it’s worth asking: Do these features actually make car seats safer? Or are parents paying for peace of mind?

I tested two smart car seats, the Babyark Classic ($799) and the Cybex Cloud G Pro ($550), to see if this technology lives up to the hype and whether a smart seat is worth adding to your registry. Because while an app-connected car seat might seem cool and offer some reassurance, no amount of technology can replace proper installation and use. Keep in mind that they’re not exactly apples-to-apples comparisons; the Babyark is a convertible car seat designed to grow with your little one, while the Cybex is an infant carrier. I tested the Babyark with my toddler daughter and the Cybex with my infant son, giving me a chance to see how each one worked at different stages of parenthood. But both offer a glimpse into how companies are integrating technology into car seats, and I wanted to see how they perform in everyday life.

Many smart car seats revolve around sensors. Some come equipped with sensors that help caregivers determine if the seat is installed correctly. Others use Bluetooth-enabled chest clips to send notifications to your phone if the chest clip breaks free mid-ride or if you walk away from your car while your child is still buckled in. A few models even have crash detection, which can send notifications to designated emergency contacts if a collision is detected.

It has been revealed that the biggest difference comes down to how the technology is integrated. Some models, like the Cybex I tested, rely on a Bluetooth chest clip that connects to an app. Babyark takes a slightly different approach, with mechanical indicators on its Classic model and a swankier electronic sensor system built into the base of its higher-end Smart and Premium models.

Industry observers note that the first thing I noticed about the Babyark out of the box was its base setup, which was different from any other car seats I’ve used. The base is a spaceship-looking device with a fold-out support leg and anti-rebound bar. The seat itself is pretty bulky, but I didn’t mind too much, since by the time I started using it, my daughter was old enough that I didn’t need to haul her around in an infant seat anymore.

Sources indicate that car seat installation can be an exercise in patience, but I found setup pretty straightforward. The Babyark app walked me through every step, with video tutorials for each stage. Once everything was in place, indicators on the base glowed green. (Red means something’s off.).

The app is easy to navigate, but once I installed the seat, I pretty much forgot about it. I enabled notifications in case something needed attention, but in my several months of using the seat, nothing has warranted an alert so far, aside from the occasional random disconnection.

According to recent reports, it’s worth noting that the Babyark offers different versions of the seat, all with different technology. The Classic model, which I have, presently retails at $790 and offers guided installation videos and mechanical indicators. Babyark's Smart and Premium models—which retail for $999 and $1,190, respectively—add features like forgotten child alerts and impact detection. That’s a roughly $200 to $400 jump, which is worth considering if you’re particularly interested in those features.

You can check the app for basic statistics, like how much time your child spends in the seat, but I haven’t felt the need to follow this closely. More importantly, I didn’t find myself opening the app to monitor the seat while my daughter was in it. At the end of the day, the Babyark feels like a regular car seat to me. But a great, sturdy car seat at that!

It has been revealed that I also tried out the Cloud G Pro, which comes with SensorSafe, a Bluetooth chest clip that communicates with the Cybex app on your phone. Pairing the clip, which looks and functions like any other, with my phone was easy peasy. When I intentionally tested the alerts, they worked as expected and came through almost immediately.

The temperature notifications worked, but almost too well. SensorSafe sends an alert when your car’s interior climbs to above 95 degrees Fahrenheit or drops below 45. Depending on the weather, your car might already be outside that range when you first get in, and it takes a little time for the cabin to warm up or cool down. So don’t be surprised if you get an alert before the AC or heat has a chance to do its thing.

SensorSafe can also alert you if the clip becomes unbuckled while driving or if you leave your child buckled in the seat and walk away with your phone. In the latter scenario, the default setting has your phone loudly announce “CHILD IN CAR!” in a man’s deep voice, which scared the hoots out of me the first time it went off. If you don’t respond to the alert (you can stop or snooze it), the app will notify your emergency contact and share your location.

Like the Babyark, I didn’t find myself opening the Cybex app very often to check on things. I mostly let it run in the background and waited for notifications rather than actively checking in on the system. The alerts worked just fine, but I used the app so infrequently that my phone eventually offloaded it.

Sources indicate that as appealing as all those gadgets and gizmos sound, car seats aren’t foolproof. “These are supplements. They're not substitutes,” notes Jennifer Booge, a car seat safety expert with the National Safety Council. “We have to make sure that we're understanding how to use the car seat correctly, because there is so much to know, and every car seat is so different.”.

According to data collected through the NSC’s National Digital Car Seat Check Form, a little over 72 percent of car seats entered into the system have some form of misuse. Manufacturers are working to address these complications with installation videos and app-based guidance, but Booge says there’s still not enough research to determine whether smart features actually improve safety.

Some car seat manufacturers offer access to certified child passenger safety technicians who can walk you through installation questions. I experienced this firsthand with the Babyark. Even after following the app’s instructions and getting the green light that everything was secure, I still had some reservations about how much the seat was wiggling. I reached out to the manufacturer, and they virtually walked me through the installation. (Which turned out to be correct; car seats are supposed to have a slight wiggle, no more than an inch back and forth.).

It has been revealed that “Don't be afraid to pick up the phone and call or schedule that virtual appointment and meet with those experts that are there to help you, because it's not easy,” Booge says. “Every car seat is different. Every vehicle and car seat combination is different.”.

As Booge points out, tech can be useful even when it isn’t built into the seat itself. The rise of virtual appointments gives caregivers access to certified technicians that they may not otherwise have available. At the end of the day, a car seat doesn’t need a battery or an app to do its job, and all the technology in the world can’t replace knowing how to use it properly.

Do you need a smart car seat? Probably not. After testing the Babyark and the Cybex Cloud G Pro with SensorSafe, I’m not totally convinced the added tech is worth paying a premium for. Both offered features I appreciated, and they certainly gave me peace of mind, but neither fundamentally changed how I use a car seat day to day. I’d rather prioritize a seat that fits my child and my vehicle, and that I can use correctly, rather than pay extra for an app I rarely open. All in all, my biggest takeaway is not to mistake more features for more safety.

#12567. Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1924 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million owners a month.
  • But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.
  • While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million owners a month.

But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.

And once installed, it’s tough to remove.

While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.

In a detailed investigation, CNN spoke to half a dozen cybersecurity teams from Asia, Europe and the United States — as well as multiple former and current Pinduoduo employees — after receiving a tipoff.

Multiple experts identified the presence of malware on the Pinduoduo app that exploited vulnerabilities in Android operating systems. Company insiders said the exploits were utilized to spy on users and competitors, allegedly to boost sales.

“We haven’t seen a mainstream app like this trying to escalate their privileges to gain access to things that they’re not supposed to gain access to,” remarked Mikko Hyppönen, chief research officer at WithSecure, a Finnish cybersecurity firm.

“This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.”.

Malware, short for malicious software, refers to any software developed to steal data or interfere with computer systems and mobile devices.

Evidence of sophisticated malware in the Pinduoduo app comes amid intense scrutiny of Chinese-developed apps like TikTok over concerns about data security.

Some American lawmakers are pushing for a national ban on the popular short-video app, whose CEO Shou Chew was grilled by Congress for five hours last week about its relations with the Chinese government.

The revelations are also likely to draw more attention to Pinduoduo’s international sister app, Temu, which is topping US download charts and fast expanding in other Western markets. Both are owned by Nasdaq-listed PDD, a multinational firm with roots in China.

While Temu has not been implicated, Pinduoduo’s alleged actions risk casting a shadow over its sister app’s global expansion.

Industry observers note that there is no evidence that Pinduoduo has handed data to the Chinese government. But as Beijing enjoys significant leverage over businesses under its jurisdiction, there are concerns from US lawmakers that any company operating in China could be forced to cooperate with a broad range of security activities.

The findings follow Google’s suspension of Pinduoduo from its Play Store in March, citing malware identified in versions of the app.

An ensuing report from Bloomberg said a Russian cybersecurity firm had also identified potential malware in the app.

Pinduoduo has previously rejected “the speculation and accusation that Pinduoduo app is malicious.”.

CNN has contacted PDD multiple times over email and phone for comment, but has not received a response.

Pinduoduo, which boasts a user base that accounts for three quarters of China’s online population and a market value three times that of eBay (EBAY), wasn’t always an online shopping behemoth.

Founded in 2015 in Shanghai by Colin Huang, a former Google employee, the startup was fighting to establish itself in a market long dominated by e-commerce stalwarts Alibaba (BABA) and JD.com (JD).

It succeeded by offering steep discounts on friends-and-family group buying orders and focusing on lower-income rural areas.

Sources indicate that pinduoduo posted triple digit growth in monthly customers until the end of 2018, the year it listed in New York. By the middle of 2020, though, the increase in monthly users had slowed to around 50% and would continue to decline, according to its earnings reports.

It was in 2020, according to a current Pinduoduo employee, that the manufacturer set up a team of about 100 engineers and product managers to dig for vulnerabilities in Android phones, develop ways to exploit them — and turn that into profit.

According to the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, the company only targeted users in rural areas and smaller towns initially, while avoiding users in megacities such as Beijing and Shanghai.

“The goal was to reduce the risk of being exposed,” they said.

By collecting expansive data on user activities, the tech giant was able to create a comprehensive portrait of owners’ habits, interests and preferences, according to the source.

This allowed it to improve its machine learning model to offer more personalized push notifications and ads, attracting people to open the app and place orders, they said.

The team was disbanded in early March, the source added, after questions about their activities came to light.

PDD didn’t reply to CNN’s repeated requests for comment on the team.

Approached by CNN, researchers from Tel Aviv-based cyber firm Check Point Research, Delaware-based app security startup Oversecured and Hyppönen’s WithSecure conducted independent analysis of the 6.49.0 version of the app, released on Chinese app stores in late February.

In a recent development, google Play is not available in China, and Android customers in the country download their apps from local stores. In March, when Google suspended Pinduoduo, it said it had found malware in off-Play versions of the app.

The researchers found code designed to achieve “privilege escalation”: a type of cyberattack that exploits a vulnerable operating system to gain a higher level of access to data than it’s supposed to have, according to experts.

“Our team has reverse engineered that code and we can confirm that it tries to escalate rights, tries to gain access to things normal apps wouldn’t be able to do on Android phones,” remarked Hyppönen.

The app was able to continue running in the background and prevent itself from being uninstalled, which allowed it to boost its monthly active user rates, Hyppönen said. It also had the ability to spy on competitors by tracking activity on other shopping apps and getting information from them, he added.

Check Point Research additionally identified ways in which the app was able to evade scrutiny.

The app deployed a method that allowed it to push updates without an app store review process meant to detect malicious applications, the researchers said.

They also identified in some plug-ins the intent to obscure potentially malicious components by hiding them under legitimate file names, such as Google’s.

“Such a technique is widely used by malware developers that inject malicious code into applications that have legitimate functionality,” they stated.

In China, about three quarters of smartphone users are on the Android system. Apple (AAPL)’s iPhone has 25% market share, according to Daniel Ives of Wedbush Securities.

Sergey Toshin, the founder of Oversecured, mentioned Pinduoduo’s malware specifically targeted different Android-based operating systems, including those used by Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi and Oppo.

CNN has reached out to these companies for comment.

Toshin described Pinduoduo as “the most dangerous malware” ever found among mainstream apps.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive,” he said.

Most phone manufacturers globally customize the core Android software, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), to add unique features and applications to their own devices.

Industry observers note that toshin found Pinduoduo to have exploited about 50 Android system vulnerabilities. Most of the exploits were tailor made for customized parts known as the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) code, which tends to be audited less often than AOSP and is therefore more prone to vulnerabilities, he said.

Recent findings suggest that pinduoduo also exploited a number of AOSP vulnerabilities, including one which was flagged by Toshin to Google in February 2022. Google fixed the bug this March, he said.

According to Toshin, the exploits allowed Pinduoduo access to people’ locations, contacts, calendars, notifications and photo albums without their consent. They were also able to change system settings and access users’ social network accounts and chats, he noted.

Sources indicate that of the six teams CNN spoke to for this story, three did not conduct full examinations. But their primary reviews demonstrated that Pinduoduo asked for a large number of permissions beyond the normal functions of a shopping app.

They included “potentially invasive permissions” such as “set wallpaper” and “download without notification,” stated René Mayrhofer, head of the Institute of Networks and Security at the Johannes Kepler University Linz in Austria.

It has been revealed that suspicions about malware in Pinduoduo’s app were first raised in late February in a report by a Chinese cybersecurity firm called Dark Navy. Even though the analysis didn’t directly name the shopping giant, the report spread rapidly among other researchers, who did name the company. Some of the analysts followed up with their own reports confirming the original findings.

Soon after, on March 5, Pinduoduo issued a fresh revision of its app, version 6.50.0, which removed the exploits, according to two experts who CNN spoke to.

Two days after the enhancement, Pinduoduo disbanded the team of engineers and product managers who had developed the exploits, according to the Pinduoduo source.

The next day, team members found themselves locked out of Pinduoduo’s bespoke workplace communication app, Knock, and lost access to files on the organization’s internal network. Engineers also found their access to significant data, data sheets and the log system revoked, the source noted.

Most of the team were transferred to work at Temu. They were assigned to different departments at the subsidiary, with some working on marketing or developing push notifications, according to the source.

A core group of about 20 cybersecurity engineers who specialize in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities remain at Pinduoduo, they said.

Toshin of Oversecured, who looked into the enhancement, said although the exploits were removed, the underlying code was still there and could be reactivated to carry out attacks.

Pinduoduo has been able to grow its user base against a backdrop of the Chinese government’s regulatory clampdown on Massive Tech that began in late 2020.

That year, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology rolled out a sweeping crackdown on apps that illegally collect and use personal data.

In 2021, Beijing passed its first comprehensive data privacy legislation.

According to recent reports, the Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that no party should illegally collect, process or transmit personal information. They’re also banned from exploiting internet-related security vulnerabilities or engaging in actions that endanger cybersecurity.

Pinduoduo’s apparent malware would be a violation of those laws, tech policy experts say, and should have been detected by the regulator.

“This would be embarrassing for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, because this is their job,” said Kendra Schaefer, a tech policy expert at Trivium China, a consultancy. “They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.”.

The ministry has regularly published lists to name and shame apps found to have undermined user privacy or other rights. It also publishes a separate list of apps that are removed from app stores for failing to comply with regulations.

Pinduoduo did not appear on any of the lists.

CNN has reached out to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Cyberspace Administration of China for comment.

On Chinese social media, some cybersecurity experts questioned why regulators haven’t taken any action.

According to recent reports, “Probably none of our regulators can understand coding and programming, nor do they understand technology. You can’t even understand the malicious code when it’s shoved right in front of your face,” a cybersecurity expert with 1.8 million followers wrote last week in a viral post on Weibo, a Twitter-like platform.

The post was censored the next day.

CNN’s Kristie Lu Stout and Sean Lyngaas contributed reporting.

Disgraced former leader Sheikh Hasina plans return to Bangladesh from exile

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former prime minister faces death penalty upon return after being sentenced in absentia over deaths in 2024 uprising.
  • Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister applied for a latest passport this week.
  • Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former prime minister faces death penalty upon return after being sentenced in absentia over deaths in 2024 uprising.

Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister applied for a latest passport this week.

Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She crossed the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.

Last November, a tribunal in Bangladesh found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death over her crackdown on a student uprising that left an estimated 1,400 people dead.

Industry observers note that her return to Bangladesh is likely to be disruptive for the country where Hasina’s party, Awami League, is still banned and thousands of its members are in jail. Should she be allowed to return, she is likely to be arrested immediately.

It has been revealed that hasina first raised the prospect of going back to Bangladesh in August. Speaking to the Guardian this week, several exiled Awami League leaders also living in India confirmed that Hasina was serious and “confident” about returning by next month. They confirmed that several other party figures had already returned in anticipation.

On Monday, a British lawyer acting on behalf of Hasina wrote to the Bangladesh high commission in Delhi requesting a new passport and national identity card to be issued “in a timely fashion”, in a letter seen by the Guardian.

“The reason our leader Sheikh Hasina has applied for a passport is that she genuinely wants to return,” said a party leader based in the Indian city of Kolkata, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he is not authorised to speak to the media on the party’s behalf.

Recent findings suggest that hasina has rejected the charges against her and claimed the tribunal that convicted her was illegitimate. “She is confident about her return, which is why she has applied for a new passport and a national identity card. If the authorities do not issue her a passport, she will apply for a travel pass to make her return to Bangladesh possible,” noted the Awami League leader.

Sources indicate that since Hasina’s conviction, the Bangladesh government has put pressure on the Indian authorities to extradite the former prime minister. However, the Indian government, which was close to Hasina while she was in power, has ignored the demands, straining ties between the two countries.

This week, the Bangladesh government mentioned that, as a “terrorist”, Hasina would only be allowed to return via an “acceptable prisoner exchange” under the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty.

Aminul Islam, the chief prosecutor of the tribunal that sentenced Hasina, said there was “no legal scope” for her to be issued a new passport as she was a “convicted fugitive”.

It has been revealed that islam emphasised that Hasina would be hanged if she returned, as the deadline for her to appeal against her conviction had passed. “Sheikh Hasina has no option but to face the execution of the verdict,” he said.

Despite the abuses and oppression that mired her 15 years in power and subsequent conviction for crimes against humanity, Hasina still commands significant popularity among the thousands of Awami League cadre still in Bangladesh, many of whom have been driven underground.

It has been revealed that analysts said they believed her decision to return was driven by an attempt to revive her support base and destabilise the newly elected government, led by Tarique Rahman. It came to power in February during Bangladesh’s first democratic election in decades.

The government has since struggled with inflation and protests that shut down garment factories, which the Awami League hopes to use to its advantage.

Another Awami League leader mentioned all those in exile intended to follow Hasina back to Bangladesh, despite many of them facing serious criminal charges and having been given lengthy prison sentences in absentia.

“Some of us have been sentenced in absentia by kangaroo courts, and we know we will be jailed. But we are ready to face the consequences and return to our own people. We will fight this politically,” mentioned the senior leader, who is based in India.

In a recent development, some senior party figures have returned in recent months, including the former MP Mustaque Ahmed Ruhi. He was immediately arrested on his return in September and faces prosecution over an alleged murder during the 2024 uprising.

Exiled Awami League leaders have continued to meet in Kolkata, where many of them are living, and are routinely summoned to Delhi to meet Hasina.

Speaking over email this week, Hasina told the Associated Press: “If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people.”.

#12561. Tesla’s Cybercab Is the Subscription Hell They Told You Not to Worry About

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (909 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla’s Cybercab Is the Subscription Hell They Told You Not to Worry About

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Or in the case of Tesla’s self-driving Cybercab, several.
  • Last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs.
  • From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is always a catch. Or in the case of Tesla’s self-driving Cybercab, several.

Last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs. The two-seat, gold vehicle is unlike any other on the market: It lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals, and is primarily driven by software. (Other autonomous vehicle companies, including Alphabet's Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox, offer self-driving rides on ride-hail networks, but don’t let people buy their cars.) Tesla’s "limited release” will supposedly offer some people (unclear how many) the opportunity to pay $29,900 to take delivery in December.

From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.

According to recent reports, the business model raises questions about what people will actually get when they buy a Cybercab. “You’ll never really own the car,” states Ivan Drury, the director of insights at Edmunds. “It’s more like $30,000 to buy into a franchise.”.

It has been revealed that according to documents posted on Tesla’s website, the vehicle “will not operate” without what Tesla is calling an “autonomy subscription," a monthly fee that will start at $299. If owners don’t pay on time and in full, their self-driving cars won’t work. If they try to operate the vehicles in areas that don’t support the service—right now, they’re restricted to portions of cities in Florida and Texas—their self-driving cars won’t work. (That area can expand, contract, or “relocate” at any time.).

If owners do anything that Tesla deems "unauthorized or inappropriate," the tech giant says it can suspend or cancel the subscription—and their self-driving cars won’t work. If the vehicle loses connectivity, the self-driving cars won’t work. (“Tesla is not responsible for carrier, spectrum, environmental, or other external outages,” its “autonomy agreement” says.).

Tesla also reserves the right to make an owner’s car not work at any time: It says it can, for any safety or security purpose, suspend or terminate access to Cybercab tech, or restrict operations by location, road type, weather, or “condition.” This is particularly salient because the Cybercab is also under investigation by US safety regulators, who are trying to understand why Tesla believes the vehicle meets safety standards without so many of the parts and systems required.

Tesla didn’t respond to a request for comment.

In a recent development, for years, automakers have seen increasingly software-dominated vehicles as an opportunity to get drivers hooked on the same special sauce that makes Netflix, Amazon, and Spotify so potent: monthly subscription services. Because these vehicles can receive over-the-air software updates, manufacturers can offer drivers new services as they make them. The upside is high, tech-style margins that keep rolling in, versus the razor-thin ones seen in car-making. A 2024 report suggested that connected-car features could one day be a $200 billion industry.

In some ways, the subscription model is working. Today, some automakers charge extra for remote start, security, internet connectivity, and advanced driver assistance features. General Motors mentioned it made $2.7 billion in subscription-related revenue last year from fees drivers paid for its OnStar and Super Cruise services.

But some customers have also found the business model yucky, or even offensive. Why charge extra to “unlock” a feature that’s already built into a car? If an automaker can add a new feature at any time, can’t they also take it away? And if they can take it away, what does "ownership" mean? In 2022, BMW told drivers in select countries it would activate factory-installed heated seats for a monthly or one-time fee; it eventually backed down after public outcry, pledging the company would no longer charge subscription fees for pre-installed hardware. (BMW is still pursuing a subscription model for some features.) “Consumers hate being nickel-and-dimed for subscriptions,” states Drury.

Recent findings suggest that tesla was an early mover in the subscription feature space and has offered connectivity and driver-assistance features for monthly or one-time fees for a decade. As the company has shifted away from making cars and toward robotics and autonomous vehicles, executives have made clear that charging for services is the future. (Its Robotaxi service currently picks up fare-paying passengers in parts of eight US cities.) So Tesla buyers may be particularly amenable to paying monthly to make their self-driving cars go.

In exchange for monthly fees, buyers will also get access to other services, too, including remote support, roadside assistance, tire, air filter, and windshield wiper replacements, and tire and camera inspections. (The agreement indicates that list might change, too.) Cybercabs will be able to “travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center,” the organization says. The fee doesn't cover insurance.

Cybercab buyers will have other restrictions. The vehicle is for personal use only. Even though CEO Elon Musk has repeatedly stated owners will be able to put their vehicles on Tesla’s wider Robotaxi network to make money during downtime, and even has an online interest form for those who want to own and operate their own Cybercab fleets, the current ownership agreement prohibits that. Buyers are also prohibited from selling or transferring their vehicles without Tesla’s written consent. The company “advises against” children under 13 riding in the Cybercab, and prohibits children from riding without an adult present.

In a post on X, Musk indicated no apparent compunction about the Cybercab business model, but did say the monthly price for autonomy “is too high.” He wrote that the price should be “more like ~$115/month.”.
